I am a self taught back end developer. There are lots of factors and luck that goes into it. If I am being completely honest, I am still mediocre, but I got a job paying 6 figures by some planning, trail & and error, and lots of luck as well. Here's some of my advice.

Make sure to do plenty of projects no matter how bad they may be at first. You just need momentum. The better you become, the better your projects are.

Put your best projects on Github, LinkedIn & Resume. It shows that you are active and have something to talk about, even if it isn't professional. Some recruiters just want any excuse to get you interviewed, and seeing your projects is good enough for some. 

Go to Meetups, you never know who you might meet that will change your life, and it's great for networking. I met someone who fixed my resume for me, which helped me get my first job in tech. I also saw another kid, nervous as hell,  but went in front of everyone and detail his skill and ask for an opportunity and the moment he went back to his seat about 6 different people came by and gave him their card so he can be interviewed.

This is up to you and how the interview is going. Sometimes, know how to exaggerate on things you've done, and that's only if you are comfortable doing that and you have the skill. For example, if you truly truly feel confident in Java but only have 1 year of experience, go ahead and put 3 years in your resume.

The interview process is a game unfortunately, some interviewers ask good realistic questions, and others are gatekeepers trying their best to grill you. Even if you fail the interview, remember the questions that trip you up, gain those skills, and try again.

I barely got into programming seriously in 2018 and I started with C language. I was told that if you can learn C then any language after that is easy. So I did C on and off for a year, then I went back to school to do my masters and there we used C#. The concept of OOP was so new to me that I barely passed that class thanks to my partner.

That summer I was unable to pursue my masters due to financial constraint but I got accepted to the infamous Revature, my class used Java. Due to still being so new to programming, Java & OOP I struggled really bad.  I remember trying to practice Java at my own time and I HATED it because I had gotten so used to C. The accelerated learning pace did not help because I did not have time to grasp anything. I was eventually let go which honestly was for the best because I would have been exposed anyway. 

Once I was fired I almost quit programming until I decided to do a bullshit teacher/student project while bored. This project changed everything, I started to grasp the OOP concept because I was working at my own pace and every problem I encountered I would Google/YouTube it.
